title: HOW ONE TINY MISTAKE SANK THE TITANIC
subject: history

beats.narration: The press called her practically unsinkable. She went down in under three hours. The iceberg? Half the story.
beats.claim: the Titanic sank in under three hours despite contemporary claims she was practically unsinkable
beats.visual_question: why did one iceberg doom a ship this size?
beats.visual_answer: the ship's own compartments, failing one by one

beats.narration: 11:40 PM, April 14. Lookouts spot the iceberg. Thirty-seven seconds later, she grazes the hull.
beats.claim: the lookouts reported the iceberg at 11:40 PM on April 14, 1912, about thirty-seven seconds before impact
beats.visual_question: how fast did the disaster unfold once spotted?
beats.visual_answer: a timeline: sighting, thirty-seven seconds, impact

beats.narration: The impact buckled hull plates across six forward compartments — not a gash, a wound the pumps could never fight.
beats.claim: the collision breached the first six forward compartments along about three hundred feet of hull
beats.visual_question: what did the iceberg actually do to the hull?
beats.visual_answer: a reconstruction of the hull with six compartments opened

beats.narration: The watertight doors slammed. But the bulkheads only rose to D deck — each compartment filled like an ice-cube tray, spilling over.
beats.claim: the watertight bulkheads rose only to D deck, so water spilled from full compartments into the next
beats.visual_question: why could the ship not simply float on the flooded compartments?
beats.visual_answer: an overflow chain: each full compartment spills into the next

beats.narration: The first drawings showed taller bulkheads. Revisions cut them by about ten feet — margin traded for roomier decks.
beats.claim: design revisions before approval lowered the watertight bulkhead height by roughly ten feet from the earlier drawings
beats.visual_answer: two designs side by side, the approved one with less margin

beats.narration: Two hours forty minutes after the collision, she was gone. About twenty-two hundred aboard — seven hundred five survived.
beats.claim: the Titanic foundered two hours and forty minutes after the collision; of roughly two thousand two hundred aboard, seven hundred and five survived
beats.visual_answer: the count: two thousand two hundred aboard, seven hundred and five saved

beats.narration: Titanic did not sink because she hit an iceberg, but because the margin that should have contained one was traded away. Her flaw, all along.
beats.claim: the loss of designed safety margin, not the iceberg alone, is what sank the Titanic
beats.visual_question: so what actually sank the Titanic?
beats.visual_answer: the ship reprised, her hull margin line lit: the flaw was built in
